Alternate translation: [And the Rabshakeh told them, “Tell Hezekiah that the great king, the king of Assyria, wants to know what this trust is that he is trusting]

The implied “you” in the imperative **say** is plural here because the Rabshakeh is addressing all three of Hezekiah’s officials. So use the plural form here in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The word **you** is singular here because the king of Assyria (speaking through the Rabshakeh) is addressing Hezekiah directly. The words “you” and “yourself” are singular in verses 20 and 21 for the same reason. So use singular forms in these verses in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The king of Assyria is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [What is this trust that you have] or [In whom are you trusting]

The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one in whom you can trust to protect you from us!]

Quote: אָמַ֨רְתָּ֙ אַךְ־דְּבַר־שְׂפָתַ֔יִם עֵצָ֥ה וּ⁠גְבוּרָ֖ה לַ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֑ה עַתָּה֙ עַל־מִ֣י בָטַ֔חְתָּ כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְתָּ בִּֽ⁠י
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that he is only speaking a word of lips when he says that he has counsel and might for war. The king asks in whom he is trusting, that he rebels against him.]

This could mean: (1) that the Assyrian king is saying Hezekiah claims to have sufficient military strength and strategy to resist, but that is mere talk. The ULT follows this interpretation. Alternate translation: [When you say, ‘I have counsel and might for war,’ that is just a word of lips] or (2) that the king is contrasting brave talk with what is actually needed for war. In that case, he would not be quoting Hezekiah. Alternate translation: [All you have is mere talk. Counsel and might are actually needed for war]

There is a fourth level of quotation here, in addition to the three that a note describes in the previous verse. According to the interpretation that the ULT follows, the king of Assyria (level 3), whom Hezekiah’s officials are to quote (level 2), as the Rabshakeh tells them to do (level 1), is quoting what he believes Hezekiah is saying (level 4). If you have decided to mark levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate punctuation in your language for this level as well.

The king of Assyria is using **a word of lips** as a common expression of his culture to mean “mere talk.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You speak only empty words] or [It is mere talk when you say]

Quote: עַתָּה֙ עַל־מִ֣י בָטַ֔חְתָּ כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְתָּ בִּֽ⁠י
Note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one you can trust to help you, that you should rebel against me]

Quote: בָטַ֣חְתָּ לְּ⁠ךָ֡ עַל־מִשְׁעֶנֶת֩ הַ⁠קָּנֶ֨ה הָ⁠רָצ֤וּץ הַ⁠זֶּה֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם
Note: The king of Assyria is speaking as if **Egypt** were actually a **broken reed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you believe that you can rely on Egypt, but that is like using a broken reed as a staff]

Quote: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמְר֣וּ⁠ן אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֣חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֖וּ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form to challenge the claim that Hezekiah’s officials might make that they are trusting in Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And you should not say to me, ‘We trust in Yahweh our God,’ since he is the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, ‘To the face of this altar in Jerusalem you shall prostrate yourselves’!]

Quote: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמְר֣וּ⁠ן אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֣חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֖וּ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: The second-level and third-level quotations that began in verse 19 conclude at the end of verse 21. There are two levels of quotation in this verse. The Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah’s officials directly (level 1), and he quotes what the officials might say and what Hezekiah has said (level 2). If you have been marking levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate punctuation in your language for the levels in this verse.

Quote: וְ⁠כִי־תֹאמְר֣וּ⁠ן אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ בָּטָ֑חְנוּ הֲ⁠לוֹא־ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵסִ֤יר חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶת־בָּמֹתָ֣י⁠ו וְ⁠אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתָ֔י⁠ו וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר לִֽ⁠יהוּדָה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֣חַ הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה תִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֖וּ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The great king says that Hezekiah should not tell him that you Judeans are trusting in Yahweh your God. After all, he is the one whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has removed and told the people of Judah and Jerusalem that they must prostrate themselves to the face of the altar in Jerusalem.]

The word **you** is plural in the first instance because the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah’s three officials. The word **you** in the second instance and the word **yourself** are plural because Hezekiah was addressing all of the Judeans. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

By **We**, Hezekiah’s officials would mean themselves and their fellow Judeans but not the Rabshakeh, to whom they would be speaking. So use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **Judah** and **Jerusalem** represent the people who live in those places. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of Judah and Jerusalem]
See how you translated the similar expression in [4:12](../04/12.md). Alternate translation: [In front of]

Quote: וְ⁠עַתָּה֙ הִתְעָ֣רֶב נָ֔א אֶת־אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י אֶת־מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְ⁠אֶתְּנָ֤ה לְ⁠ךָ֙ אַלְפַּ֣יִם סוּסִ֔ים אִם־תּוּכַ֕ל לָ֥⁠תֶת לְ⁠ךָ֖ רֹכְבִ֥ים עֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [And now, please invite Hezekiah to make a wager with my master, the king of Assyria. Tell him that I will give him 2,000 horses if he is able to put riders on them for himself]

This is the beginning of something that the Rabshakeh is saying directly to Hezekiah. He implicitly wants the Judean officials to quote to Hezekiah what he says. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in your translation. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah from me, ‘And now]

**And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce an important point such as the implications of what they were just saying. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. See how you translated this expression in [3:23](../03/23.md).

The implied “you” in the imperative **wager** and the pronouns **you** and **yourself** are singular in each instance because the Rabshakeh is addressing Hezekiah directly. The words “you” and “yourself” are singular in verse 24 for the same reason. So use singular forms in these verses in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Quote: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְּטַנִּ֑ים וַ⁠תִּבְטַ֤ח לְ⁠ךָ֙ עַל־מִצְרַ֔יִם לְ⁠רֶ֖כֶב וּ⁠לְ⁠פָרָשִֽׁים
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [But ask him how he would turn back the face of a captain of one of the least servants of my master. Tell him I know that is why he is trusting for himself in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen]

Quote: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְּטַנִּ֑ים
Note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But even then, you would not be able to turn back the face of a captain of one of the least servants of my master!]

Quote: וְ⁠אֵ֣יךְ תָּשִׁ֗יב אֵ֠ת פְּנֵ֨י פַחַ֥ת אַחַ֛ד עַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנִ֖⁠י הַ⁠קְּטַנִּ֑ים
Note: The Rabshakeh is using one part of a person, his **face**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But how would you turn back a captain of one of the least servants of my master] or [But how would you force a captain to retreat even if he was one of the least servants of my master]

The Rabshakeh is using the possessive form to describe a **captain** who would be **one of the least servants** of the king of Assyria, that is, one of his weakest soldiers. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a captain who was among the least servants of my master]

This is the end of what the Rabshakeh is saying directly to Hezekiah. In the next verse, the Rabshakeh quotes the end of the message from Sennacherib that he wants the officials to give to Hezekiah. If you have been marking levels of quotation with punctuation, use the appropriate closing punctuation at the end of this verse.

Quote: עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לְ⁠הַשְׁחִת֑⁠וֹ יְהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י עֲלֵ֛ה עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את וְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָֽ⁠הּ
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah that the king of Assyria says that he has not come up against this place to destroy it without Yahweh. Yahweh told him to go up against this land and destroy it]

Quote: עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לְ⁠הַשְׁחִת֑⁠וֹ יְהוָה֙ אָמַ֣ר אֵלַ֔⁠י עֲלֵ֛ה עַל־הָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את וְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָֽ⁠הּ
Note: There are four levels of quotation in this verse. If you have decided to mark levels of quotation with punctuation, see what you did in the similar case of the four levels in verses 19 and 20.

Quote: עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לְ⁠הַשְׁחִת֑⁠וֹ
Note: This is the beginning of something that Sennacherib is saying directly to Hezekiah. It is the rest of the message that the Rabshakeh began to quote in verses 19–21. The Rabshakeh implicitly wants the Judean officials to quote this to Hezekiah as something that Sennacherib has said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this in your translation. Alternate translation: [Say to Hezekiah, ‘Thus says the great king, “Now have I come up]

Quote: עַתָּה֙ הֲ⁠מִ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה עָלִ֛יתִי עַל־הַ⁠מָּק֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לְ⁠הַשְׁחִת֑⁠וֹ
Note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not think that I have come up against this place to destroy it without Yahweh!]

Sennacherib is not using the phrase **without Yahweh** to mean that Hezekiah should not think that he has come without Yahweh accompanying him. Rather, he means that he has come after receiving a command from Yahweh. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [without receiving a command to do so from Yahweh]

Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah are speaking of themselves in the third person as **your servants** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to us, your servants,]

Quote: דַּבֶּר־נָ֤א אֶל־עֲבָדֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ אֲרָמִ֔ית כִּ֥י שֹׁמְעִ֖ים אֲנָ֑חְנוּ
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since we, your servants, understand Aramaic, please speak to us in that language]

Eliakim is using the name of the dialect of Hebrew that people spoke in the kingdom of Judah. Some versions use the name of the language rather than the name of this dialect and say “in Hebrew.” If you have decided to use the same names in your translation that the biblical author does, you may wish to use the name Judean here. If not, you may wish to use the name Hebrew here.

Here, **ears** represent “hearing.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the hearing of the people who are on the wall] or [, since the people who are on the wall can hear us]

Quote: הַ⁠עַ֨ל אֲדֹנֶ֤י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אֵלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ שְׁלָחַ֣⁠נִי אֲדֹנִ֔⁠י לְ⁠דַבֵּ֖ר אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֑לֶּה הֲ⁠לֹ֣א עַל־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים הַ⁠יֹּֽשְׁבִים֙ עַל־הַ֣⁠חֹמָ֔ה לֶ⁠אֱכֹ֣ל אֶת חרי⁠הם וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׁתּ֛וֹת אֶת־שיני⁠הם עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם
Note: The Rabshakeh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My master did not send me to speak these words only to your master and to you! He also sent me to speak them to the men sitting on the wall, who will eat their dung and drink their urine with you!]
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:7](../01/07.md). Alternate translation: [this message]

Even though the author says that the Rabshakeh spoke to **them**, the word **your** and the word **you** in its first instance are singular because the Rabshakeh is replying directly to Eliakim, who spoke on behalf of all three Judean officials. The word **you** in its second instance is plural because the Rabshakeh is including Shebnah and Joah in what he says will happen. Use the appropriate singular and plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The author probably does not mean that the Rabshakeh had been sitting down and having a private conversation with the Judean officials and that he then **stood** up. If the conversation had been private, there would have been no need for Eliakim to ask him to speak in Aramaic so that the people on the wall would not understand. So the author probably means that the Rabshakeh stood in such a way that his speech to the people on the wall would seem even more forceful and intimidating. Alternate translation: [And the Rabshakeh assumed a dominating stance]
See how you decided at [1:10](../01/10.md) to represent the phrase **and said** when it introduces a direct quotation.

Quote: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ אַל־יַשִּׁ֥יא לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי־לֹ֣א יוּכַ֔ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדֽ⁠וֹ
Note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the multiple levels of quotation in verses 19–25. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate all of this long quotation so that there are not quotations within quotations. Alternate translation: [The king says that you should not let Hezekiah deceive you, since he is not able to deliver you from his hand]

Quote: אַל־יַשִּׁ֥יא לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי־לֹ֣א יוּכַ֔ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדֽ⁠וֹ
Note: Some ancient manuscripts read “his hand.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “my hand.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Quote: אַל־יַשִּׁ֥יא לָ⁠כֶ֖ם חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּי־לֹ֣א יוּכַ֔ל לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם מִ⁠יָּדֽ⁠וֹ
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since Hezekiah is not able to deliver you from my hand, do not let him deceive you]

The word **you** is plural in both of these instances because king of Assyria, speaking through the Rabshakeh, is addressing the Judeans who have gathered on the city wall. For the same reason, the words “you” and “your” and the implied “you” in imperatives are also plural throughout verses 30–32. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Quote: וְ⁠אַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְ⁠כֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ אֶת־הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
Note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. The Rabshakeh is quoting the king of Assyria (level 2), also continuing from the previous verse. The king is quoting Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

Quote: וְ⁠אַל־יַבְטַ֨ח אֶתְ⁠כֶ֤ם חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֣ה לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר הַצֵּ֥ל יַצִּילֵ֖⁠נוּ יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ אֶת־הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [The king says that you should not let Hezekiah make you trust in Yahweh by telling you that delivering, Yahweh will deliver all of you, and this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria]

According to the king of Assyria, Hezekiah has been repeating forms of the verb **deliver** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will certainly deliver us]
By **us**, Hezekiah means to include both himself and those to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction, here and in verse 32.

The expression **will not be given** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will not give this city]
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:10](../03/10.md). Alternate translation: [into the control of]
To translate the term “listen” here and in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expression in [10:6](../10/06.md). Alternate translation: [Do not do what Hezekiah wants you to do here]

Quote: כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֗וּר עֲשֽׂוּ־אִתִּ֤⁠י בְרָכָה֙ וּ⁠צְא֣וּ אֵלַ֔⁠י וְ⁠אִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵֽנָת֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵֽי־בוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [the king of Assyria is telling you to make a blessing with him and come out to him. Then you will be able to eat, a man of his vine and a man of his fig tree, and drink, a man from the waters of his well]

Here, **a blessing**, meaning a gift, represents “a peace agreement,” since in this culture people exchanged gifts when they made peace agreements. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Make a peace agreement with me]

Quote: וְ⁠אִכְל֤וּ אִישׁ־גַּפְנ⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ תְּאֵֽנָת֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁת֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ מֵֽי־בוֹרֽ⁠וֹ
Note: See how you translated the similar expression in [3:23](../03/23.md). Alternate translation: [and let each of you eat from his vine and fig tree, and let each of you drink from the waters of his well]

Quote: עַד־בֹּאִ⁠י֩ וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֨י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֜ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּ⁠אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֗ם אֶרֶץ֩ דָּגָ֨ן וְ⁠תִיר֜וֹשׁ אֶ֧רֶץ לֶ֣חֶם וּ⁠כְרָמִ֗ים אֶ֣רֶץ זֵ֤ית יִצְהָר֙ וּ⁠דְבַ֔שׁ וִֽ⁠חְי֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א תָמֻ֑תוּ וְ⁠אַֽל־תִּשְׁמְעוּ֙ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ כִּֽי־יַסִּ֤ית אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר יְהוָ֖ה יַצִּילֵֽ⁠נוּ
Note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what the Rabshakeh said (level 1), continuing from the previous verse. The Rabshakeh is quoting the king of Assyria (level 2), also continuing from the previous verse. The king is quoting Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

Quote: עַד־בֹּאִ⁠י֩ וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֨י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֜ם אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּ⁠אַרְצְ⁠כֶ֗ם אֶרֶץ֩ דָּגָ֨ן וְ⁠תִיר֜וֹשׁ אֶ֧רֶץ לֶ֣חֶם וּ⁠כְרָמִ֗ים אֶ֣רֶץ זֵ֤ית יִצְהָר֙ וּ⁠דְבַ֔שׁ וִֽ⁠חְי֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א תָמֻ֑תוּ וְ⁠אַֽל־תִּשְׁמְעוּ֙ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ כִּֽי־יַסִּ֤ית אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר יְהוָ֖ה יַצִּילֵֽ⁠נוּ
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [until he comes and takes you to a land like your land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive of oil and honey. He tells you to live and not die. He says that you should not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you by telling you that Yahweh will deliver all of you]
Since the rest of the items on this list are agricultural products, these **vineyards** may represent the products of vineyards. Alternate translation: [and grapes]

The phrase **olive of oil** describes cultivated olives, that is, olives from trees in orchards as opposed to wild olives, which yielded less and worse oil. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [cultivated olives]

Quote: הַ⁠הַצֵּ֥ל הִצִּ֛ילוּ אֱלֹהֵ֥י הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֖ם אִ֣ישׁ אֶת־אַרְצ֑⁠וֹ מִ⁠יַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
Note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. # 2 Kings 19 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

The story of Hezekiah continues in this chapter. He is one of the great kings of Judah, so the author is describing his reign in detail.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Sennacherib’s sons kill him?

The author reports in 19:37 that after Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, while he was worshiping in the temple of the Assyrian god Nisrok, Adrammelek and Sharezer, two of his sons, assassinated him. They did that because of a bitter conflict over who would succeed him as king, as ancient Assyrian sources report. The crown prince Assur-nadin-shumi died, and Sennacherib at first named Adrammelech his heir. But later he replaced him with Esarhaddon, a younger son, for reasons that the sources do not specify. This made Adrammelek very angry, but Sennacherib refused to reinstate him. So he conspired with his brother Sharezer to assassinate their father. They had hoped to seize power for themselves, but they had to flee, and Esarhaddon became the next king.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

As in chapter 18, there are two long quotations in this chapter that contain multiple levels of quotation. They are in verses 10–13 and 20–34. Notes describe ways of indicating the speakers throughout these quotations. See what you did in the case of the quotations in the previous chapter, and present these quotations in the same way.

### Images in the king of Assyria’s boast

In 19:23, Yahweh uses vivid imagery to depict how the Assyrian king has been boasting of his military conquests. Here is an explanation of the various images that he uses.
- As Yahweh quotes him, Assyrian king is speaking as if he had actually gone up the highest and most remote mountains of **Lebanon** and cut down its tallest and most valuable trees.
- He is using **Lebanon** to represent the entire geographical area of which Israel is a part.
- He is using the giant **trees** that grow in Lebanon to represent huge, strong entities, so that his boast to have cut them down means that he has defeated powerful foes.
- By **the lodging place of its end**, he means the place where his army would stop at the end of a successful campaign to conquer the whole country, that is, Jerusalem. (The author says in [18:13](../18/13.md) that Sennacherib sought first to conquer all of the other fortified cities in Judah, and then he attacked Jerusalem.)
- By **the forest of its garden** (that is, its forest that is like a garden), he means the place where the forest has been most transformed by cultivation into a park for human recreation and enjoyment. This seems to represent the grounds of the royal palace and temple, particularly in light of how extensively cedar and cypress wood was used in the construction of those buildings.
Consider how best to represent these images in your translation. A note to this verse suggests one possible way to do that.

Quote: זֶ֣ה הַ⁠דָּבָ֔ר אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה עָלָ֑י⁠ו בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם

The people of Jerusalem shake their heads after you]

Quote: בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם

The people of Jerusalem will shake their heads after you]

Quote: בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: Yahweh, speaking through Isaiah, is speaking to someone whom he knows cannot hear him, the king of Assyria. He is doing this to communicate to Hezekiah that he feels very strongly about that king’s arrogance and mockery. If it would be helpful in your language, here and through verse 28, you could translate these words as if Yahweh were speaking directly to Hezekiah about the king of Assyria. The daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head after him] or [The people of Jerusalem will despise him, they will deride him. The people of Jerusalem will shake their heads after him]

In this culture, shaking or wagging one’s head at a person was a symbolic action by which people showed contempt and expressed mockery toward that person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [The daughter will shake her head disdainfully and mockingly after you]

Isaiah assumes that his listeners will know that by **after you**, he means that the Assyrians will flee from Jerusalem and that the people of the city will make this gesture at them as they run away. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at you as you flee] or [at him as he flees]

Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh asks him whom he has mocked and taunted. Yahweh asks him against whom he has raised a voice and lifted his eyes upward. The answer is that he has done that against him, the Holy One of Israel!]

Quote: אֶת־מִ֤י חֵרַ֨פְתָּ֙ וְ⁠גִדַּ֔פְתָּ וְ⁠עַל־מִ֖י הֲרִימ֣וֹתָ קּ֑וֹל וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֥א מָר֛וֹם עֵינֶ֖י⁠ךָ
Note: Yahweh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You must realize whom have you mocked and taunted! You must realize against whom have you raised a voice and lifted your eyes upward!]

The action of **lifting** his **eyes upward** was a symbolic action by which the king of Assyria showed arrogance and defiance toward Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and arrogantly lifted your eyes upward] or [and defiantly lifted your eyes upward]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to describe the holy God with whom the Israelites are in a covenant relationship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the holy God with whom you Israelites are in a covenant relationship]

Quote: בְּ⁠יַ֣ד מַלְאָכֶי⁠ךָ֮ חֵרַ֣פְתָּ ׀ אֲדֹנָ⁠י֒ וַ⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר ב⁠רכב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְח֣וֹר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָב֨וֹאָה֙ מְל֣וֹן קִצֹּ֔⁠ה יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
Note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Isaiah told Hezekiah in his message (level 1), continuing from the previous verses. This includes what, according to Isaiah, Yahweh was saying to Hezekiah, also continuing from the previous verse (level 2). This includes a quotation from the king of Assyria (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

Quote: בְּ⁠יַ֣ד מַלְאָכֶי⁠ךָ֮ חֵרַ֣פְתָּ ׀ אֲדֹנָ⁠י֒ וַ⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר ב⁠רכב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְח֣וֹר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָב֨וֹאָה֙ מְל֣וֹן קִצֹּ֔⁠ה יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that by the hand of his messengers he mocked him and said boastfully that with the multitude of his chariotry, he went up to the height of the mountains, the recesses of Lebanon. He boasted that he cut down the heights of its cedars, the choicest of its cypress trees, that he might enter the lodging place of its end, the forest of its orchard]

Quote: ב⁠רכב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְח֣וֹר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָב֨וֹאָה֙ מְל֣וֹן קִצֹּ֔⁠ה יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
Note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the elaborate comparison that the Assyrian king is drawing in this verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I commanded my chariot forces and invaded this land, even though it was remote from me and secure. I defeated the most powerful and skillful opponents. Now I am going to enter Jerusalem and capture the royal palace and temple]
See how you translated the similar expression in [9:36](../09/36.md). Alternate translation: [Through the agency of your messengers]

The Assyrian king is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I went up** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is boasting. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and said boastfully, “With the multitude of my chariotry, I went up]

Quote: אֲנִ֣י קַ֔רְתִּי וְ⁠שָׁתִ֖יתִי מַ֣יִם זָרִ֑ים וְ⁠אַחְרִב֙ בְּ⁠כַף־פְּעָמַ֔⁠י כֹּ֖ל יְאֹרֵ֥י מָצֽוֹר
Note: This verse is the conclusion of the third-level quotation that begins in the previous verse. If you have decided to use punctuation to mark levels of quotation, end this verse with the appropriate punctuation for closing a third-level quotation.

Quote: אֲנִ֣י קַ֔רְתִּי וְ⁠שָׁתִ֖יתִי מַ֣יִם זָרִ֑ים וְ⁠אַחְרִב֙ בְּ⁠כַף־פְּעָמַ֔⁠י כֹּ֖ל יְאֹרֵ֥י מָצֽוֹר
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that the Assyrian king has boasted that he has dug wells and drunk foreign waters. He has also boasted that he will dry up all of the streams of Matsor with the sole of his feet]

The Assyrian king is stating the pronoun **I** explicitly, even though the verb translated as **I dug** already includes this meaning, because he is boasting. See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse.

The Assyrian king could be saying: (1) that he was able to dig wells and drink water from them in **foreign** countries. This would be a boast that his armies could successfully traverse arid, desolate areas. (Compare how the Israelite army and its allies nearly perished of thirst in [3:9–10](../03/09.md).) Alternate translation: [I have wells in foreign countries and drank water from them] or (2) that he was able to dig wells and find water in places where no one suspected it would be. This might be a taunt at Hezekiah, who, according to [2 Chronicles 32:3–4](../2ch/32/03.md), tried to eliminate the supply of water around the city of Jerusalem to thwart the Assyrians. Alternate translation: [I have been able to dig wells and find water in places my enemies did not expect]

The word **Matsor** is another name for Egypt. (The word is related to the word for “border.” Egypt was considered the border of Israel.) Alternate translation: [And with the sole of my feet I will dry up all of the streams of Egypt]

In this verse, the word **sole** is singular in form, but the king is using it to refer to both of his feet. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural or dual form of “sole.” Alternate translation: [And with the soles of my feet I will dry up all of the streams of Egypt]

The king is speaking as if he could actually **dry up all the streams of** Egypt with the soles of his **feet**, the way a person could stamp out a small puddle. The **streams** of Egypt, meaning the Nile and its tributary, represent something formidable, like the giant trees of Lebanon in the previous verse. The king is boasting that after conquering Jerusalem, he will conquer the Egyptian empire without great effort. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And next I will conquer Egypt without great effort]

Quote: הֲ⁠לֹֽא־שָׁמַ֤עְתָּ לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי לְ⁠מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִֽ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ עַתָּ֣ה הֲבֵיאתִ֗י⁠הָ וּ⁠תְהִ֗י לַ⁠הְשׁ֛וֹת גַּלִּ֥ים נִצִּ֖ים עָרִ֥ים בְּצֻרֽוֹת
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that the Assyrian king must surely have heard that from long ago, he did it, that from days of antiquity, he formed it. Now Yahweh has brought it, that the king should be for devastating fortified cities into ruined heaps]

Quote: הֲ⁠לֹֽא־שָׁמַ֤עְתָּ לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי לְ⁠מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִֽ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ
Note: Yahweh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely you must have heard that from long ago, I did it, that from days of antiquity, I formed it]

Quote: לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי לְ⁠מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִֽ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ
Note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I decided a long time ago that this would happen]
See how you translated the similar expression in [10:36](../10/36.md). Alternate translation: [from ancient times]

The expression **ruined** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [into heaps of ruins]

Quote: וְ⁠יֹֽשְׁבֵי⁠הֶן֙ קִצְרֵי־יָ֔ד חַ֖תּוּ וַ⁠יֵּבֹ֑שׁוּ הָי֞וּ עֵ֤שֶׂב שָׂדֶה֙ וִ֣⁠ירַק דֶּ֔שֶׁא חֲצִ֣יר גַּגּ֔וֹת וּ⁠שְׁדֵפָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י קָמָֽה
Note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that their dwellers are short of hand, they feel dismay and feel shame. They are vegetation of the field or green of herb; grass of roofs, blasting to the face of growing up]

Yahweh is using **short of hand** as a common expression of this culture to mean “powerless.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are powerless]

Quote: הָי֞וּ עֵ֤שֶׂב שָׂדֶה֙ וִ֣⁠ירַק דֶּ֔שֶׁא חֲצִ֣יר גַּגּ֔וֹת וּ⁠שְׁדֵפָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י קָמָֽה
Note: Yahweh is speaking as if the people whom the Assyrians are conquering are actually tender plants that are defenseless against certain threats. Plants growing in the **field** can be easily trampled, for example, while **grass** growing on the flat **roofs** of this culture could easily wither in the heat of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. # 2 Kings 20 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the author concludes his detailed account of the reign of Hezekiah, one of the great kings of Judah.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Isaiah say to put figs on Hezekiah’s sore?

In the ancient world, figs were a known remedy for sores and boils. Figs contain natural compounds and enzymes that have anti-inflammatory, soothing, and drawing effects. These can help bring a festering boil to a head and reduce swelling and infection. However, Hezekiah was so ill that he was near death, so it was improbable that the effects of the figs alone would have cured him. So agreeing to have his servants put the figs on his sore anyway was therefore an act of faith, trust, and obedience by Hezekiah. It showed that he was prepared to follow the instructions of Yahweh’s prophet, even if it did not seem that the measures he specified would be sufficient. Isaiah had the king’s servants use the best means available, so that they and he and the king were doing their part. But Hezekiah ultimately had to trust Yahweh for his healing.

# 2 Kings 21 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the author continues to tell what the kings were like who ruled over the kingdom of Judah.

  1. King Manasseh of Judah (1–18)
  2. King Amon of Judah (19–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### How could such a good king as Hezekiah have had such a bad son as Manasseh?

The author says in 18:5 that Hezekiah “trusted in Yahweh the God of Israel” more than any of the kings of Judah who lived before him or after him. By contrast, he says that Hezekiah’s son Manasseh was even more evil than the pagan nations that had lived in Canaan before the Israelites. How could such a good king have had such a bad son? Manasseh was only 12 years old when his father died and he became king. He was still young and impressionable, and he seems to have come under the influence of a group of Judean leaders who had consistently opposed Hezekiah’s reforms. The book of Isaiah describes how these leaders continued to worship foreign gods and cultivate foreign alliances (Isaiah 2:6–9, 20:5, 30:1–7). They seem to have done all they could to influence Manasseh to become like them and, unfortunately, they seem to have succeeded.

# 2 Kings 22 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the story of Josiah, another of the great kings of Judah. Because he is so important, the author describes the history of his reign at length, in chapters 22 and 23.

# 2 Kings 23 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, the author concludes the story of Josiah, and he then continues to tell what the kings were like who ruled the kingdom of Judah.

  1. King Josiah of Judah (22:1–23:30)
  2. King Jehoahaz of Judah (23:31–35)
  3. King Jehoiakim of Judah (23:36–24:7)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Neco not want Jehoahaz to be king?

Pharaoh Neco removed Jehoahaz from being the king of Judah because, for one thing, he wanted to show that he was the one who was in control of that kingdom. By picking the next king himself and changing his name, Neco was telling the Judeans, “You must not make your own king without my permission.” Neco also may have believed that Jehoahaz would have been a stronger and more independent ruler, so he made his brother Eliakim the king instead. This was Neco’s way of making sure Judah stayed weak and under his rule.

### How did Jehoahaz get to Riblah?

The Bible does not say exactly how Jehoahaz got to Riblah, where Pharaoh Neco put him in prison. Some interpreters suggest that Neco summoned Jehoahaz and so Jehoahaz went to Riblah by himself, hoping to show respect or obedience to Pharaoh. Others suggest that Pharaoh Neco’s soldiers captured Jehoahaz and brought him to Riblah as a prisoner because Neco had ordered them to do that. Either way, Jehoahaz appeared before Neco at Riblah, in the region of Hamath, where Neco deposed him as king and made him his prisoner.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The Mount of Destruction

In 23:13, when the author refers to the “Mount of Destruction,” he is making a word play on the name of that mountain. Because olive trees grew there, and because olive oil was used for anointing, it was known as the Mount of Anointing. The author changes one vowel and an “h” to a “th” in the word for “anointing” to get a word that means “destruction.” He is calling the mountain by that name in order to emphasize that the corrupt worship represented by the pagan shrines that Solomon built there led to the destruction of the kingdom. If you have decided to use the same names that the author does in each place in the book, you may want to say “the Mount of Destruction” in your translation. However, since it is difficult to translate a play on words in one language into another language, you may want to call this mountain by its familiar name, the Mount of Olives, so that your readers will know that the author is referring to that mountain near Jerusalem. You could explain in a footnote what name the biblical author uses in Hebrew.

The pronoun **they** refers to messengers whom King Josiah **sent** out. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the king sent out messengers who gathered to him]
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:3](../01/03.md). Alternate translation: [And the king went]
See how you translated the similar expression in [5:18](../05/18.md). Alternate translation: [to the temple of Yahweh]

The author is saying **every** and **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and people from throughout Judah and the various parts of Jerusalem]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and every man and woman of Judah]

The author is providing a further description of the crowd of people from **Judah** and **Jerusalem** who gathered at the temple. By naming two extremes, **small** and **great** (poor and rich, or ordinary and powerful, or young and old), he means those extremes and everything in between. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [including people from a wide range of ages and classes]
See how you translated the similar expression in [18:26](../18/26.md). Alternate translation: [in their hearing]

The expression **having been found** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that Hilkiah had found]

The author says in [11:14](../11/14.md) that it was a “custom” for a new king to stand “by the pillar,” apparently a certain one of the pillars on the temple porch, as a visible sign of his loyalty to Yahweh. Josiah had already been the king for 18 years, but he was now symbolizing that he and his people were making a new start by together pledging their loyalty to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And the king stood by the pillar to show that he and his people were making a new start]
See how you translated the similar expression in [11:4](../11/04.md). Alternate translation: [and he made a covenant]
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:14](../03/14.md). Alternate translation: [in the presence of Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in [8:18](../08/18.md). Alternate translation: [to live as Yahweh wished]

The terms **commandments**, **testimonies**, and **statutes** mean similar things. The author is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all of his commandments]

The author is referring to all of a person by naming two major components of a person, his **heart** and his **soul**. These represent overlapping aspects of the inner life of a person, representing a person’s thoughts, feelings, desires, and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in [1 Kings 2:4](../1ki/02/04.md). Alternate translation: [wholeheartedly] or [with his entire being]

The author is speaking as if the **words of this covenant** were objects that Josiah could **raise up**. He means that Josiah pledged to make happen what the covenant said should happen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in [1 Kings 2:4](../1ki/02/04.md). Alternate translation: [to make happen what the covenant said] or [to bring the covenant back into effect]

The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that that scroll recorded]

The author is using **stood in the covenant** as a common expression of his culture to mean “agreed to the covenant” or “became parties to the covenant.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all of the people joined in the covenant] or [And all of the people agreed to the terms of the covenant]

The expression **having been made** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that previous kings had made] or [that previous kings had commanded their workers to make]
See how you translated the similar expression in [17:16](../17/16.md). Alternate translation: [and for all the lights in the sky] or [and for the heavenly bodies]

Bringing the **ashes** of the burned idolatrous objects to the city of **Bethel**, which was outside the borders of Judah but under Judean control, was a symbolic action by which Josiah showed that he wanted no trace of these objects to remain in his kingdom. Furthermore, since idolatry in Israel had begun when Jeroboam placed a calf image in Bethel, this was a symbolic way of sending idolatry back to where it began in order to end it definitively. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he sent their ashes out of Judah to Bethel, where Israel’s idolatry had begun]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [to the sun and to the moon and to the constellations, yes, to the whole army of the heavens]

Since any contact with a dead body, including walking over a grave, made a person ceremonially unclean ([Numbers 19:16](../../num/19/16.md)), throwing the **dust** of the **Asherah** pole that had been in the temple onto a **grave** was a symbolic action by which Josiah rendered the remains of this object unclean and completely unsuitable for use in worship. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he threw its dust over the grave of the sons of the people to make it defiled]

In this verse, the word **grave** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the graves in this area outside Jerusalem. It appears that people who could not afford a tomb cut into rock were buried in a common plot there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “grave.” Alternate translation: [the graves of]
See how you translated the similar expression in [2:16](../02/16.md). Alternate translation: [the common people]

Quote: אֲשֶׁ֣ר הַ⁠נָּשִׁ֗ים אֹרְג֥וֹת שָׁ֛ם בָּתִּ֖ים לָ⁠אֲשֵׁרָֽה
Note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. You can do the same with the similar expression in the next verse. Alternate translation: [where women were weaving houses for Asherah]

Quote: אֲשֶׁ֣ר הַ⁠נָּשִׁ֗ים אֹרְג֥וֹת שָׁ֛ם בָּתִּ֖ים לָ⁠אֲשֵׁרָֽה
Note: Since actual **houses** are not something that people make by **weaving**, the author seems to be using the term to represent something else. Interpreters are not entirely sure what this was, but many suggest that these were either fabric coverings for images of Asherah or small, decorated tents representing dwellings for Asherah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could suggest one of these meanings in your translation. You could also use a general expression. Alternate translation: [where women wove coverings for Asherah images] or [where women did weaving for Asherah]

The author is referring to all of the territory of Judah by naming two extremes, the city of Geba at its northern edge and the city of Beersheba in the far south. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout the territory of Judah]

The author is using the expression **high places** to represent the kind of shrines that people built on high places, that is, on hilltops. Since these were in cities, at their **gates**, they would not necessarily have been in the highest location in a given area. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the gate shrines]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the gate**, he means the main gate of Jerusalem. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the main gate of the city]

Quote: אַ֗ךְ לֹ֤א יַֽעֲלוּ֙ כֹּהֲנֵ֣י הַ⁠בָּמ֔וֹת אֶל־מִזְבַּ֥ח יְהוָ֖ה בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם כִּ֛י אִם־אָכְל֥וּ מַצּ֖וֹת בְּ⁠ת֥וֹךְ אֲחֵי⁠הֶֽם
Note: The author is providing background information about the priests he described in the previous verse. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Quote: לֹ֤א יַֽעֲלוּ֙ כֹּהֲנֵ֣י הַ⁠בָּמ֔וֹת אֶל־מִזְבַּ֥ח יְהוָ֖ה בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם
Note: Not allowing the **priests** who had previously served at the **high places** was a symbolic action by which Josiah kept any trace of false worship away from the Jerusalem temple. These priests were descendants of Aaron who had been burning incense to Yahweh, but they had been doing so at unauthorized locations. This worship was therefore impure, and those who had led the people in it had to be kept away from Yahweh’s altar. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

The author is using **go up to the altar** as a common expression of his culture to mean “offer sacrifices on the altar.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [serve at the altar of Yahweh] or [offer sacrifices on the altar of Yahweh]

The author is using one kind of food that the priests received as their share of sacrifices, the **unleavened bread** that they made from grain offerings, to mean all of the food that the priests received from sacrifices for their support. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [However, they were allowed to live off the food from the priests’ share of the sacrifices]

The author is speaking as if the other priests were actually the **brothers** of these priests who had been serving at hilltop shrines. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [together with their fellow priests]

Quote: לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֗י לְ⁠הַעֲבִ֨יר אִ֜ישׁ אֶת־בְּנ֧⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־בִּתּ֛⁠וֹ בָּ⁠אֵ֖שׁ לַ⁠מֹּֽלֶךְ
Note: See how you translated the similar expression in [16:3](../16/03.md). Alternate translation: [so that no one could burn up his son or his daughter completely as an offering to Molech]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can use an expression that would be natural. Alternate translation: [And he burned up the chariots of the sun]

This could mean: (1) that these **altars** were on the **roof** of an **upper chamber** that **Ahaz** had built somewhere in the palace complex. Alternate translation: [that were on the roof of the upper chamber of Ahaz] or (2) that these **altars** were on the **roof** of the palace, near an **upper chamber** that **Ahaz** had built. Alternate translation: [that were on the palace roof near the upper chamber of Ahaz]

Quote: וַ⁠יָּ֣רָץ מִ⁠שָּׁ֔ם וְ⁠הִשְׁלִ֥יךְ אֶת־עֲפָרָ֖⁠ם אֶל־נַ֥חַל קִדְרֽוֹן
Note: The verbs **ran** and **threw** together express a single idea. The word **ran** tells in what way Josiah removed the dust and **threw** it into the Kidron Valley (or had his servants do this). If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And he hastened to have their dust thrown into the Valley of Kidron]
See how you translated the similar expression in [4:12](../04/12.md). Alternate translation: [that were in front of Jerusalem] or [that were opposite Jerusalem]

The author is speaking of directions in the way characteristic of his culture, in which people described directions as if a person were facing east, toward the sunrise. The south would be to the right of such a person. So the author means these **high places** were on the south side of the mountain. Alternate translation: [that were on the south side of]
See the discussion of this name in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [the Mount of Olives]
See how you translated the similar expression in [8:12](../08/12.md). Alternate translation: [the Ammonites]

Since contact with a dead body caused ritual uncleanness, putting human bones on the sites of these high places made them unsuitable for any further use in worship. See how you explained the significance of Josiah’s similar action of scattering the dust of the vessels of Baal and Asherah on human graves in [23:6](../23/06.md).
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:7](../01/07.md). Alternate translation: [according to the message from Yahweh]

Quote: אֲשֶׁ֤ר קָרָא֙ אִ֣ישׁ הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר קָרָ֔א אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֖ים הָ⁠אֵֽלֶּה
Note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [about these things that the man of God had proclaimed]

The men of the city are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [That monument is the grave of the man of God]

Josiah is using two phrases to say basically the same thing, first positively and then negatively. The repetition emphasizes the idea that the phrases convey. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Let no one disturb his bones at all]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [So the men of the city rescued his bones]

To translate the name **Samaria**, meaning the northern kingdom of Israel, here and in the next verse, see how you decided to represent it in [17:24](../17/24.md). Alternate translation: [the prophet who was from the northern kingdom]
See how you translated the similar expression in [5:18](../05/18.md). Alternate translation: [the shrines on high places]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **provoking anger**, he means that the **kings of Israel** provoked Yahweh’s anger when they made these shrines. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [provoking Yahweh’s anger]

The author does not mean that Josiah **sacrificed** these **priests** to Yahweh. He did not offer them on these **altars** as human sacrifices. Rather, he means that Josiah slaughtered them right on their pagan altars as if they had been sacrifices. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And he slaughtered]

The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [as this scroll of the covenant specifies]

The author is providing background information to help readers understand the significance of what Josiah did in this instance. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **had not been done** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one had observed the Passover in this way]
See how you translated the similar expression in [10:36](../10/36.md). Alternate translation: [from the time of the judges]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [the Israelite judges]

Quote: כִּ֗י אִם־בִּ⁠שְׁמֹנֶ֤ה עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה לַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ יֹֽאשִׁיָּ֑הוּ נַעֲשָׂ֞ה הַ⁠פֶּ֧סַח הַ⁠זֶּ֛ה לַ⁠יהוָ֖ה בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
Note: If it would appear in your language that the author was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement, combining verses 22 and 23. Alternate translation: [The only occasion on which the Israelites celebrated Passover during the whole time that the judges judged Israel and kings ruled in Israel and Judah was in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, when the people of Jerusalem observed Passover for Yahweh]

The expression **was done** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the people observed this Passover]
See how you translated these expressions in [21:6](../21/06.md).

The term **teraphim** describes idols that people in this culture kept in their homes. If your readers would not be familiar with what these were, in your translation you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a general expression. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in [1 Samuel 15:23](../1sa/15/23.md). Alternate translation: [and the household idols]

The author is using the term **seen** in a way characteristic of his language and culture to mean that these **abominations** could be seen, that is, they were present in **Judah** and **Jerusalem**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the comparable expression “that was found” in [20:13](../20/13.md). Alternate translation: [that were]
See how you translated the similar expression in [23:3](../23/03.md). Alternate translation: [in order to bring back into effect]
See how you translated the similar expression in [23:3](../23/03.md). Alternate translation: [that the scroll recorded]
See how you translated the similar expression in [17:2](../17/02.md). Alternate translation: [before him]
See how you translated the similar expression in [23:3](../23/03.md). Alternate translation: [energetically with his entire being]

The author is speaking as if a later king might have physically **arisen**, or gone up into the air or to an elevated location. In contexts such as this, this expression describes a person assuming a powerful position. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in [1 Kings 14:7](../1ki/14/07.md). Alternate translation: [one like him has not come to power] or [one like him has not reigned]

Quote: לֹֽא־שָׁ֣ב יְהוָ֗ה מֵ⁠חֲר֤וֹן אַפּ⁠וֹ֙ הַ⁠גָּד֔וֹל אֲשֶׁר־חָרָ֥ה אַפּ֖⁠וֹ בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֑ה
Note: See how you translated the similar expression in [13:13](../13/13.md). Alternate translation: [Yahweh remained very angry with the anger that he felt against Judah]

Quote: לֹֽא־שָׁ֣ב יְהוָ֗ה מֵ⁠חֲר֤וֹן אַפּ⁠וֹ֙ הַ⁠גָּד֔וֹל אֲשֶׁר־חָרָ֥ה אַפּ֖⁠וֹ בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֑ה
Note: The author is using a construction in which a verb (**burned**) and its object (**burning**) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, whether or not you retain some or all of the image in your translation, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s anger continued to burn greatly against Judah] or [Yahweh continued to feel very great anger against Judah]

In this instance as well, the author is using a construction in which a verb (**provoked**) and its object (**provocations**) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [all that things that Manasseh had done that made him angry]

Quote: וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה גַּ֤ם אֶת־יְהוּדָה֙ אָסִיר֙ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל פָּנַ֔⁠י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֲסִרֹ֖תִי אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
Note: The author seems to be rephrasing what Yahweh said in [21:13](../21/13.md), “I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria.” So it would be appropriate to use a verbal form in your language, as the ULT does, that shows that this is something Yahweh had said in the past, not something that he said even after Josiah made all of his reforms.
See how you translated the similar expression in [13:23](../13/23.md). Alternate translation: [away from this land]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [I said that my name would be there]
See how you translated the similar expression in [21:7](../21/07.md). Alternate translation: [It will be a special place for people to worship me]

Quote: וְ⁠יֶ֛תֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י יֹאשִׁיָּ֖הוּ וְ⁠כָל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֑ה הֲ⁠לֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה
Note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is concluding the story of Josiah. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar phrases in [1:18](../01/18.md).
See how you translated the similar expression in [8:20](../08/20.md). Alternate translation: [During his reign]

In this context, the word **meet** has the sense of “oppose.” Josiah was not coming to greet or support Neco but to fight him in order to keep him from marching his army through Judean territory. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to oppose him]
The pronoun **he** refers to Neco, while the pronoun **him** refers to Josiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but Neco killed Josiah]

In this context, the word **saw** has the sense of “encounter.” Josiah and Neco did not have a face-to-face meeting at or after which Neco killed Josiah. When their armies fought, Josiah was killed in the battle. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when he encountered him]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people such as Josiah’s **servants** or soldiers, who are the subject in the previous sentence. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And he was buried] or [And people buried him]

Quote: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְ⁠שָׁלֹ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ יְהוֹאָחָ֣ז בְּ⁠מָלְכ֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה חֳדָשִׁ֔ים מָלַ֖ךְ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְ⁠שֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔⁠וֹ חֲמוּטַ֥ל בַּֽת־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ מִ⁠לִּבְנָֽה
Note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is introducing **Jehoahaz** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in [8:26](../08/26.md).
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:2](../03/02.md). Alternate translation: [And he did what Yahweh considered to be evil]
See how you translated the similar expression in [8:24](../08/24.md). Alternate translation: [his ancestors]
See how you decided to represent the weight of a kikkar in [5:5](../05/05.md).

Changing Eliakim’s name was a symbolic action by which Neco asserted his sovereignty over Judah and its ruler. (Since Eliakim means “God will establish” while Jehoiakim means “Yahweh will establish,” it is possible that Neco allowed Eliakim to choose his own new name. The symbolic significance was in the fact that Neco forced him to change his name.) If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he changed his name to Jehoiakim to assert his sovereignty over him]

Here, **the land** represents the people who lived in the land of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but he assessed the people of the land] [but he determined how much each person should pay]

Here, Pharoah’s **mouth** represents what he said by using his mouth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the amount of silver that Pharaoh had demanded]

# 2 Kings 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

  1. King Zedekiah of Judah (24:18–25:7)
  2. Destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians (25:8–21)
  3. The remaining Judeans flee to Egypt (25:22–26)

In this chapter, by completing his account of the reign of Zedekiah, the author concludes the story of the kings who ruled the kingdom of Judah. He also concludes the entire story that is told throughout the books of 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings. That is the story of how the Israelites of both kingdoms disobeyed Yahweh so seriously that Yahweh allowed enemies to conquer them and take them into exile away from their land. As the author describes the conquest and destruction of Judah and the exile of its people, he does not say specifically that this was the result of the people breaking their covenant with Yahweh, as he did in the case of the northern kingdom in 17:7–23. That is because he has already made that point by quoting Yahweh’s decree of judgment in 21:10–15 and saying in 23:26 that Yahweh did not rescind that decree even after the thorough reforms of Josiah. The overall message of this long historical account is nevertheless clear. Yahweh was not at fault when the Israelites were conquered and exiled from their land. Instead, this happened because the people disobeyed Yahweh and broke their covenant with him.

Since the author says in the next verse that “all the people” fled to Egypt after this, he does not mean here that Ishmael and his men killed all of the “people having been left in the land of Judah” mentioned in verse 22 who were living in the area of Mizpah.
